steps.content: The idea is about yesterday's move: coins with a large downward close-to-previous-close return should bounce, so the factor should be high for coins that fell. The simplest, unit-free form is the negative of the one-day return. I'll test that first.

The one-day return has essentially zero incremental IC (t = 1.2) — it is essentially the short-term reversal signal, which is already stripped out. So the plain one-day return carries nothing new. Next I try the same idea measured as position within the coin's own recent range: where today's close sits between its own lowest and highest of the past five days, negated so that coins closing far below their range score high.

The position-in-own-range version is worse (−0.0059, t = −2.8), so it is mostly noise and its own volatility, not a new signal. Since the one-day return is the literal statement of the idea and it fails incrementally, I stop here rather than spend the last test on a window or smoothing variant of the same signal.

What I found: the direction is right (rank IC +0.0175), but the signal is entirely absorbed by the known styles — the incremental IC is 0.0000 with all three sub-periods at 0.0000. So on this history the bounce is not a residual effect; it is the reversal signal already contained in the one-day return, and averaging or expanding the window cannot recover it. I keep the plain, simplest form pointing the way the idea says.

The idea is about the size of yesterday's move, measured as a ratio so coins of different price units are comparable, and the sign is positive because a big one-day drop should bounce. My first test is the simplest version: the log return over the past one day.

The one-day return has exactly zero incremental IC (t = −0.7) — it is the short-term reversal style, which is already removed, so its raw rank IC is just noise. To keep the same direction but measure yesterday's move in a less noisy way, I will use the position of the close inside the day's range (ln(high/low) − ln(close)), which is bounded and less driven by two- endpoints.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The range position is a ratio, so it is also unit-free, but it is also extremely noisy: dividing by (high − low) leaves a gap at the day where high = low, and a single wick can dominate a whole day. Next I rank coins each day across the range before averaging over the window, which keeps the magnitude but removes a few extreme days.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

Two forms of the same thing failed to add anything: the plain one-day return (0.0000, t = −0.7) and its rank-then-average version (also 0.0000, because ranking each day collapses to a few coins with the same value). That is two tests in a row without a 0.002 improvement, so I stop here.

What I found: the signal is entirely in the known reversal style — the one-day return has rank IC −0.0175 but incremental IC 0.0000, so almost nothing survives after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed. The direction is the one the idea states (bigger one-day drop → higher factor), and it holds in every sub-period (2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 −0.0000), but the magnitude is well under 0.002, so the bounce is not measurable at this horizon. The plain version is the simplest and least noisy, so I hand that in.

What I found: measured as average trade size in USDT (log of `quote_volume`), the level is nearly entirely absorbed by the liquidity style — only −0.0057 survives, and its t = −4.9 means it is weakly and consistently *against* the idea in all three periods (2022H2 −0.0097, 2023 −0.0065, 2024 −0.0028). The 5-day horizon is too short to escape the volatility/reversal styles, and stretching the window to 20 days or measuring the jump against a 20-day baseline made it worse, so the plain level is the best of the three. The direction is as the idea states (bigger average trade size → lower value), and I keep it that way rather than flipping the sign to chase the signal.

That is a large jump: +0.0195 with t = 7.9, and all three periods positive (+0.031, +0.017, +0.016). So measuring the close as a share of the day's range works, while the plain difference-to-low-position mean did not — the mean is dominated by a few extreme wide bars, whereas the ratio is bounded and those bars sit at the top.

I stop here: the third variant (ratio, median) failed to beat the second by 0.002, so the ratio over the five-day window with min_periods = 4 is the one to hand in. Direction is as the idea states — coins closing near the high get a high value.

The idea is about the range, measured as high minus low, which is unit-free and therefore comparable across coins. Since wide range is bearish, the factor takes the negative of the average range over a few days. I start with the simplest version: log of high/low, averaged over 5 days.

The 5-day mean has an essentially zero absolute IC (0.0003) but a large negative incremental IC (−0.0079) with t = −2.4, and all three periods are negative — so the level of range is almost entirely absorbed by volatility, which is the largest style. The mean is still dominated by a few wide-range days, so next I try the same quantity measured with medians (robust, less sensitive to single wide bars) over a longer 10-day window.

The 10-day median is worse (−0.0084, t = −2.5), so lengthening the window did not help — the signal is too short-lived to escape the volatility style. Since a few extreme bars dominate the mean, one more robust measurement is the rank of each day's range inside the coin's own history, then averaged over 5 days: this ignores the magnitude of a single bar and keeps only the order of wide vs narrow days.

That third test is the best of the three: incremental IC +0.0009 (t = 0.4), only 0.0008 above the 5-day mean, but it is the only one with all three periods non-negative (2022H2 +0.0023, 2023 +0.0026, 2024 −0.0014). The gain is far below the 0.002 that would justify another round, and two tests in a row failed to improve on the best by 0.002, so I stop here.

What I found: the level of the high-low range is almost entirely volatility, so its incremental IC is near zero, and its direction is the opposite of the idea — coins with wide ranges did slightly *better*, not worse, over the next days (rank IC ≈ 0, so the effect is not a volatility-driven reversal in this sample). Using medians and coin-own ranks instead of means did not help enough to justify the extra complexity, so the simplest form is what I hand in, with the direction the idea states (wide range → low factor value).

The idea is about the size of the daily high-low range, which is (high − low)/close, a ratio so it is unit-free and comparable across coins. Wide range should be bearish, so the factor takes the negative of the average range over the recent days. I start with the simplest form: a 5-day mean of the log range, using log differences so single coins with tiny ranges don't dominate.

The idea is about the gap between close and open, measured as a ratio so it is comparable across coins of very different price levels. The plainest first form is the log of that ratio, averaged over a few days to reduce one-off noise.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The ratio is nearly zero for coins that closed at their open, so many coins fall out of the log — that is why it fails. The rank-based version keeps every coin in the window by ranking the gap inside its own cross-section each day and then averaging, which removes the zero-value coins.
error: lag(): periods must be a positive integer
The lag must be an integer, so I write it as a one-day return (close over close a day ago).
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

Both rank and log forms still collapse on days when the close sits exactly at the open. The plain ratio is zero in those cases, so many coins contribute nothing and the mean is unstable. The third form measures the gap in log units but ranks it *within each coin first* (rank in its own cross-section each day), then averages over the window. This keeps every coin in the sum and lets only size-driven coins dilute it.

That computes: incremental IC +0.0057 with t = 2.2, and the direction is as the idea states — coins closing above their open do outperform. The rank-within-coin transformation was the key fix: it removes the days where close = open and lets every coin contribute a real number rather than a zero, which lifted the mean from nothing to 0.0057.

The period profile is weak (2023 is nearly flat at +0.0022), so the effect is weak and mostly sits in 2022H2 and 2024; it is also much smaller than the 0.01–0.03 mark, so it is not a strong signal. Since the plain log ratio is the simplest form that keeps every coin in the sum, I stop here rather than spend a test on smoothing or a different window.

The idea is about yesterday's own move: coins that closed far below their open (a bearish move) should bounce, so the factor is minus the one-day return. Since the direction is "bigger fall → higher value", the outer `-1` sits on the return. Using log returns keeps coins with wide range days comparable to coins with narrow ones.

The plain one-day return has essentially zero incremental IC — its entire rank IC is carried by the short-term reversal style, which is subtracted out. So the raw signal is all already known style. To keep the same idea but remove the single-day noise, I'll measure the fall as the position of the close inside the day's range (log(1 − close/open)), which is bounded and less driven by a single print, then average it over three days.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The rank version fails because a single day's range position is the same for nearly every coin — dividing by open/close collapses to a single number for coins with a narrow range, so there are too few distinct values to rank. That is a shape problem, not a direction problem: the idea is about yesterday's own move, so the plain return is the right measure, but it is too noisy to survive the style removal. Since the one-day return is exactly the style that gets subtracted, I'll try the two-day return instead, which is a different measurement of the same idea (still one day of lag, but averaged).
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

Two days also collapses to a single number for most coins, so that fails too. That leaves the three-day version: averaging the log return over three days keeps the same idea (the size of the coin's move yesterday, with coins that fell large scoring high) while averaging out one noisy day.

Direction is as the idea states — bigger fall, higher value — and I keep the minus sign outside so that big falls score high.

The most direct measurement is log dollar volume, since it is scale-free (log of USDT volume, so coins of different price units compare equally) and avoids the huge-volume coins dominating. I'll start with the simplest version — log of quote_volume averaged over 5 days, negated so low volume scores high.
